before: RAII means Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: an owning object acquires a resource during construction and releases it during destruction. A destructor is named ~ClassName and takes no arguments.

This Trace is a lifecycle illustration, not an actual file owner. Its constructor/destructor print when a nested scope begins and ends. Real standard-library owners use this lifetime mechanism to release memory or close handles.

Use standard containers and smart pointers instead of hand-writing ownership code. Automatic objects are destroyed in reverse construction order on normal scope exit. Cleanup destructors should not allow failures to escape.

Expected output or behavior: enter
work
leave
after
. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Create two named trace objects and observe the reverse destruction order. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: A resource is something a program uses and must release, such as memory or an open file. RAII is the C++ pattern of putting that responsibility in an object. When the owner is destroyed, it releases its resource.
A destructor runs when an object is destroyed. Its name is the class name with ~ in front, and it takes no arguments. Standard containers and smart pointers already use destructors to manage cleanup.
Trace only prints messages so you can see an object's lifetime. It does not open a file or own another resource. The constructor prints enter; the destructor prints leave.
The program prints enter, work, leave, and after on separate lines. marker is destroyed at the closing brace of the inner block, before after prints.

Returning normally from a function also destroys its ordinary local objects. They are destroyed in reverse construction order. Abruptly stopping the whole process does not give the same cleanup guarantee.
